items.summary: State is a data structure holding the event stream (chronological past actions and observations, including user interactions) plus auxiliary information such as accumulated LLM cost and delegation metadata.
items.notes: Design description by authors; not a measured result.

items.summary: Core actions: IPythonRunCellAction and CmdRunAction execute Python and bash inside the sandbox; BrowserInteractiveAction drives a web browser through the BrowserGym domain-specific language.
An agent is implemented through a step function mapping the current state to an action; Figure 3 gives a minimal example.
For each task session a docker container sandbox is started; actions are executed through a REST API server inside it (the action execution API); a workspace directory is mounted.
The API server maintains a bash shell, a Jupyter IPython server and a Playwright-based Chromium browser; browser observations include HTML, DOM, accessibility tree, screenshot and opened tabs.

Runtime supports arbitrary docker images by building an image that installs the action execution API; images carry a hash-based tag (MD5 of the build folder) and a generic tag; build reuses an existing image, else rebuilds from the latest generic image, else builds from scratch.

AgentSkills is a Python package of utility functions auto-imported into the IPython environment; a skill is added only if (1) it is not readily achievable for the LLM to write code directly and/or (2) it involves calling an external model. Examples: edit_file, scroll_up, scroll_down, parse_image, parse_pdf.
AgentDelegateAction lets one agent delegate a subtask to another; example: the generalist CodeActAgent delegates web browsing to the specialised BrowsingAgent.

AgentHub agents: CodeActAgent (default generalist, CodeAct framework), Browsing Agent (zero-shot prompting), GPTSwarm Agent (optimizable graphs), and micro agents (specialised prompts reusing a generalist implementation).

Adoption figures stated by authors: 32K GitHub stars, more than 2.1K contributions from over 188 contributors; MIT license; agent hub with over 10 implemented agents; evaluation framework supports 15 benchmarks.

Table 2 lists the 15 integrated benchmarks in three categories: Software (SWE-Bench, HumanEvalFix, BIRD, BioCoder, ML-Bench, Gorilla APIBench, ToolQA), Web (WebArena, MiniWoB++), Misc. Assistance (GAIA, GPQA, AgentBench, MINT, Entity Deduction Arena, ProofWriter).

Evaluation setup details: SWE-Bench results without hint text and Lite subset by default; ML-Bench on the quarter subset; ToolQA easy subset; BioCoder with original context-carrying prompts removed; BIRD 300 dev samples with multi-turn interaction; MINT up to five iterations; ProofWriter uses logical forms provided by Logic-LM; MiniWoB++ full set; baselines are open-source reproducible ones without benchmark-specific manual prompt engineering.

Authors' summary of evaluation: OpenHands agents may not achieve top performance in every category; the same CodeAct agent without modifications to its system prompt is competitive across software development, web interaction and miscellaneous tasks; 26% on SWE-Bench Lite is competitive with other open-source SWE specialists; BrowsingAgent is competitive among agents using LLMs with domain-general prompting.

items.summary: Authors: 'Current agents still struggle with complex tasks'; interest in building better agents through training and inference-time techniques.
Authors: 'Current agent suffers a lot when editing long files'.
Authors: 'OpenHands's workflow still requires a substantial handcrafted workload'; graph-based frameworks such as GPTSwarm and LangGraph are proposed as alternatives.

Authors list future directions: principled multi-modality (images, video via browser; XLSX via code) and integrating Auto Eval & Refine (retry-on-error with Reflexion prompts and task completion reward models) into the browsing agent.

Ethics statement: most AI agents today are research artifacts lacking reliable long-horizon ability; risks noted; OpenHands is said to mitigate risk by (1) enabling systematic evaluation, (2) facilitating human-agent interaction rather than unsupervised autonomy, (3) giving researchers access to agents for safety research.

Integration tests: end-to-end tasks compared against a gold file; LLM calls intercepted and answered from stored prompt-response pairs matched exactly; pairs regenerated with real LLMs on breaking changes; tests scheduled per pull request and commit across Linux and Mac and local, SSH and exec sandboxes.

Graphical user interface shows the agent's actions (browsing, bash, Python), lets users view files and interrupt the agent at any moment to give feedback; connected to the event stream and agnostic to agent and runtime.

Runtime workflow (client-server via docker): user supplies base image; OpenHands builds runtime image with runtime client; container launched; backend sends actions over REST and receives observations; the client executes actions, manages working directory and loaded plugins.

Related-work statements by authors: LangChain and LangGraph provide building blocks with basic runtime support; CrewAI focuses on orchestrating multi-agent communication and offers sandboxed but limited code interpreter features; AutoGen implements Python and bash execution with stateless command execution; BrowserGym targets web browsing; DSPy emphasizes end-to-end prompt optimization; AutoCodeRover and SWE-Agent target software engineering.

Table 1 compares frameworks on domain, graphical user interface, standardized tool library, built-in sandbox and code execution, built-in web browser, multi-agent collaboration, human-AI collaboration, AgentHub, evaluation framework and agent QC (quality control); domains: SWE for AutoCodeRover and SWE-Agent, General for the others including OpenHands.

items.summary: Authors list five features: event-stream interaction mechanism; docker-sandboxed runtime with bash, browser and IPython; agent interface for creating/editing software, executing code and browsing; multi-agent delegation; evaluation framework.

Authors envision OpenHands as a catalyst for future research innovations and diverse applications; conclusion states the platform accelerates research innovations and real-world applications of agentic AI systems.

Benchmarks repository README: evaluation infrastructure for OpenHands agents; benchmarks listed as SWE-Bench, SWE-Bench Pro, GAIA, Commit0, OpenAgentSafety, ProgramBench (all marked Active); migration in progress from OpenHands V0 to the OpenHands Software Agent SDK (V1); each benchmark run is configured with an LLM configuration file.

Benchmarks repository README: two workspace types. Docker workspace (local containers, suited to development and small-scale evaluations); remote workspace (runtime API provisioning containers, pre-built images per SDK commit, parallelism such as 32+ concurrent workers). Not every benchmarks version is compatible with every SDK version.

Agent Canvas README: self-hosted control center for coding agents and automations; runs OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini or any Agent-Client-Protocol agent; local, Docker, VM or cloud backends; automations triggered on schedule or webhooks; status badge beta.

Agent Canvas README architecture: powered by the OpenHands Agent Server, a REST API for running multiple agents on one machine; each Agent Server runs on a single host/port and the frontend can switch between servers; multi-repository system with separate repositories for the frontend, the SDK/Agent Server, a TypeScript client and automations.
Contribution process: point-based authorship tracked in units of pull requests.
